title: The Nature of the Church
summary: This part addresses the local church. The church is not a consumer service but a family that gathers around covenant and exists to produce mature sons; “family shows up.” God’s glory is defined not as a mystical cloud but as His intention made manifest, Jesus become flesh and humanity itself, so the whole earth filled with glory means people knowing who they are. The local church, modelled on the Roman strategy of an ekklēsia governing a colony, is the hope of the world, and it functions by discerning the body: regarding no one according to the flesh, honouring authority, and preserving (not creating) the unity that already exists in heaven. It ends with John the Revelator, said to have no death record because he discerned the resurrected Christ and the resurrected bride.
thesis: The thriving local church, a family that shows up and sees one another as God sees them rather than according to the flesh, is heaven’s strategy for filling the earth with God’s glory.

flow.text: Many churches but few healthy ones; people get hurt, and churches have become consumer‑driven places people visit for a fix.
The church exists to produce mature sons, not to meet needs; families gather around covenant, being registered in heaven together, not around need.
The preacher honours the host pastors as rare apostolic parents the congregation may take for granted.
Moses, who already spoke with God face to face, asked to see His glory; God hid him in the rock (Christ) and showed His “back parts,” read as times past: creation itself.
God’s glory is His intention manifest, Jesus made flesh, and you; so the earth filled with glory means people knowing who they are, and the church must affirm humanity.
God appoints apostolic fathers over regions (metron); impartation requires showing up, as Paul wanted to visit Rome.
Jesus borrowed Roman terms: apostles sent from the kingdom set up an ekklēsia (governing assembly) to turn a colony into the kingdom; the Lord’s Prayer is this strategy.
The new commandment makes love transcendent: we recognise one another as God recognises us, loved with the Father’s love for the Son.

flow.step: Regard no one according to the flesh
flow.text: Since one died for all, all died; we must see each other as new creation, as the risen Christ, not by genetics or history.
Weakness, sickness and death come from not discerning the body; Nazareth’s familiarity with Jesus cost them miracles.
Power comes from God, but authority holds the local church together; Jesus was authorised by His younger‑in‑ministry cousin John.
Unity already exists in heavenly Zion; we preserve it by looking past doctrines and preferences and gathering around family, not agreement.
Acts 2 shows large apostolic gatherings plus homes for fellowship with people you like; both are needed.
John saw the risen Christ and the bride, fell down both times, wrote “as He is so are we,” and (it is claimed) has no death record.

teachings.title: Healthy local churches are rare
teachings.body: The preacher’s county has 93,000 people, 226 churches and 25 bars, yet few people join a local assembly without getting hurt. It takes a particular leadership to build a culture of family rather than organisation.

teachings.title: Don’t take local apostolic fathers for granted
teachings.body: Respected new‑creation teachers worldwide point to the host pastors as a voice to connect with. People who can drive ten minutes to such a church often don’t realise how fortunate they are.

teachings.title: “When we all show up”
teachings.body: Pastors commonly describe their size by who comes when everyone attends. A pastor in a video told his church he is not their drug dealer: families don’t gather around need or drop in for a fix; families show up.

teachings.title: The church’s purpose: producing sons
teachings.body: The church became consumer‑driven, and what lives by the sword dies by it. The church exists to produce sons of God to the measure of the stature of Christ’s fullness, equipped for ministry; it is not required to be a charity.

teachings.title: Church confronts and changes you
teachings.body: If you treat church as an organisation to meet your needs you will always be disappointed. It exists to confront, challenge and change you and to give accountability.

teachings.title: Gather around covenant
teachings.body: Being registered in heaven together is why you belong together. As a family you take responsibility for a city and its metron, and you show up.

teachings.title: Define glory God’s way
teachings.body: Glory is often equated with misty clouds or felt presence, but those are encounters. Moses asked God to show His glory, so we should accept God’s own answer; a sparkly cloud covering the earth would not be impressive.

teachings.title: God looks at you
teachings.body: Scripture says God cannot look upon sin, and Western tradition concludes He cannot look at us. But He is looking at you, so you are not defined as sin.

teachings.title: Moses in the rock
teachings.body: Moses already spoke with God face to face as a friend, yet asked to see His glory. God put him in the rock, which is Christ, the Word through whom all things were made, and showed him His back parts, which the preacher says in Hebrew means times past.

teachings.title: Glory is God’s intention manifest
teachings.body: God showed Moses, from inside the Son, the act of creation itself. God’s glory is His intention made manifest, Jesus become flesh, and you. God is human‑affirming, and the church must be too.

teachings.title: Ministry of reconciliation affirms humanity
teachings.body: The pinnacle of 2 Cor 5 is that God was in Christ reconciling the world, not counting trespasses. That ministry is one of affirming humanity, and God’s glory is His creation, the capstone being humanity.

teachings.title: Earth filled with glory = people knowing who they are
teachings.body: If the end goal of the gospel is that all people become the manifestation of the Godhead, the fullness of God, then the earth filled with His glory is less about a giant worship service and more about people understanding their identity.

teachings.title: The local church is the hope of the world
teachings.body: Not the church in general but the local church. God appointed apostolic fathers over regions; Paul called this a sphere (metron). Each takes full responsibility for their area, evicting what is illegal in heaven and bringing in heaven’s family, nature and culture.

teachings.title: Impartation requires presence
teachings.body: Romans is the most significant and articulate letter on God’s intent and covenant, yet Paul says he must come to Rome to impart a gift and bear fruit. Even the best teaching (or livestream or online course) does not replace relational impartation, which only happens if you show up.

teachings.title: Ekklēsia was a governing term
teachings.body: Ekklēsia was not a religious word; it meant a governing assembly, more courthouse than sanctuary, which took responsibility for its region and set things in order. We have “baptised” the word into something religious.

teachings.title: Rome’s colony strategy
teachings.body: Unlike Egypt, which plundered and grew only at home, Rome won population, wealth and territory by sending apostles (sent ones) from the kingdom to set up an ekklēsia in a conquered place, replacing its government so the colony became like the kingdom. Jesus’ young followers would have understood this mission.

teachings.title: The Lord’s Prayer as kingdom strategy
teachings.body: Jesus taught prayer in these terms: thy kingdom come in the colony as in the kingdom. The tactic for redeeming creation is thriving local churches that feel like family and look like heaven.

teachings.title: The greatest commandment answered the question asked
teachings.body: Asked for the greatest law in the Law and Prophets, Jesus gave love of God and neighbour. Since Jesus fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, the preacher says that statement is now null; Jesus answered only what He was asked.

teachings.title: The new commandment: love as He loved
teachings.body: The only time Jesus tells us what to do is His new commandment to love as He has loved us. Love becomes transcendent rather than reciprocal: we recognise one another as He recognises us. The Father loves us with the same love He has for the Son, and that is the bar for the body.

teachings.title: Church hurt reduces identity
teachings.body: A local counselling office deals almost wholly with church hurt. Churches put people under religion and shrink their identity: a man under a bridge is told he is not just an addict but a sinner.

teachings.title: One died for all, therefore all died
teachings.body: We dislike the word “all,” but Paul says if one died for all then all died. Jesus took away the world’s sin, and sons must now apply the finished work to creation.

teachings.title: Regard no one according to the flesh
teachings.body: This is subtler than it sounds: Jesus Himself was a victim of being seen according to the flesh. The disciples once knew Him as a carpenter’s son but saw the Transfiguration and the risen Christ, and know Him that way no longer. If anyone is in Christ, new creation.

teachings.title: Weak, sick and dying from not discerning the body
teachings.body: Paul’s warning is applied to failing to see one another as God created us, while staying full of judgment, bitterness and hurt. The person beside you is like the risen Christ of Revelation 1; if they don’t know it, it is your responsibility to make that real to them.

teachings.title: Nazareth: astonished to offended
teachings.body: In His hometown the people were first astonished at Jesus’ wisdom, then someone noted He was the carpenter’s son with family present, and they took offence. Seeing Him by genetics and environment as a mere man cost them: He could do no mighty work there.

teachings.title: Honour unlocks impartation
teachings.body: Not discerning the body means not realising what others carry and not giving honour, so you cannot receive their gifting. Familiarity alone does not breed contempt; familiarity plus immaturity does.

teachings.title: Power versus authority
teachings.body: Power comes from God; authority does not, and authority is what holds the local church together. At 30 Jesus needed to be recognised as a rabbi, so He went to His cousin John, only six months into ministry, to be baptised to fulfil all righteousness: empowered by His Father, authorised by His cousin.

teachings.title: “By what authority?”
teachings.body: The religious leaders accepted where Jesus’ power came from but asked who authorised Him. Jesus asked about John’s baptism; when they refused to answer, He would not answer, because they would not affirm the man who authorised Him.

teachings.title: Submission without hierarchy
teachings.body: The Creator stepped into a local body and asked what He could do, a picture of family. Jesus overcame familiarity by submitting to His cousin, not because of hierarchy but because both knew who the other was in the heavenlies.

teachings.title: You cannot create unity
teachings.body: Creating unity is a losing battle: denominations leave their doctrines at home and agree on something empty, as with joint prayer events hedged by rules about songs and communion. You cannot gather around doctrine or agreement; you gather around family.

teachings.title: Unity must be preserved
teachings.body: Paul says to keep the unity of the Spirit. The church is already resurrected in heaven; Zion has no denominational walls, only the church of the firstborn and the spirits of the righteous made perfect. That unity existed before the world began; we preserve it by looking past pet doctrines, preferences and attitudes.

teachings.title: Relational incompatibility is fine
teachings.body: Some believers are simply incompatible; large early churches (Jerusalem with 3,000 on the first day, Ephesus said to number 26,000) did not all get along. It is fine to keep your distance.

teachings.title: Big gatherings plus house churches
teachings.body: Acts 2 shows teaching under the apostles in large gatherings and homes for breaking bread, gladness, favour and simplicity of heart with friends. A small church that ignores its city misses the point; both regional apostolic fathers and homes are necessary.

teachings.title: John the Revelator discerned the body
teachings.body: The preacher claims John has no death record among the twelve, that Jesus said he would not die, and that attempts to kill him failed. He saw the risen Christ (dated AD 68) and the destruction of every enemy, and fell down as dead before the risen Christ and again before the bride, the Lamb’s wife.

teachings.title: As He is, so are we
teachings.body: John returned to write that love is perfected among us and that as He is, so are we in this world. He called himself the Beloved because he knew his resurrected self, discerned the body, and brought heaven’s Zion unity into the natural local church. Family shows up.

stories.title: “I’m not your drug dealer”
stories.text: The preacher had just told someone his church size “when we all show up” when he saw a video of a pastor telling his church he was not their drug dealer and that families don’t gather around need. A week later another pastor gave the same “when we all show up” answer. The point: church is family, not a service you visit when you need a fix.

stories.title: The host pastors
stories.text: He describes the host couple, with five children, a thriving business and church, and great energy and hospitality, as the most impressive leaders he has met. He urges the congregation not to take their local apostolic parents for granted.

stories.title: Counselling office for church hurt
stories.text: A counselling office in his town works almost entirely with people hurt by churches. Churches can shrink people’s identity, telling a man living under a bridge he is not just an addict but a sinner.

stories.title: Ecumenical prayer events
stories.text: Joint prayer days where churches leave their doctrines at home and can’t sing fast or slow songs or take communion illustrate how forced unity settles on something empty.

stories.title: The man he couldn’t get along with
stories.text: He once sat with a man and admitted they had nothing to talk about and simply didn’t click. This shows relational incompatibility is normal, and house fellowship lets people spend time with those they like.

stories.title: Nazareth’s offence
stories.text: In Mark 6 the hometown crowd went from astonished to offended once they recalled Jesus’ family, and so saw few miracles. Familiarity with immaturity blocks impartation.

stories.title: Jesus baptised by His cousin
stories.text: Jesus, the Creator, submitted to His cousin John, who was only months into ministry, to be authorised; this models honour in the local body.

stories.title: Moses hidden in the rock
stories.text: God hides Moses in the cleft of the rock and lets him see His back, presented prophetically as Moses being placed in the Son and watching creation come into being.

words.lexicon: Back, rear, hinder side; as an adverb “backward” and sometimes “afterward/hereafter” (e.g. Isa 41:23, 42:23). In Exod 33:23 it contrasts with God’s face, so “back” is the plain sense. A temporal sense exists but leans toward “later,” not “past.”

words.claimed: Paul’s “sphere”: a region an apostolic father and church are responsible to turn into heaven.
words.lexicon: Measure, measuring rule, allotted portion; in 2 Cor 10:13–15 the “measure” or limit of the field God assigned to Paul (with kanōn). A geographic assignment is a fair reading there; applying it to every local church is an extension.

words.claimed: Not a religious term: a governing assembly, more courthouse than sanctuary, used by Rome to govern colonies.
words.lexicon: An assembly; in Greek cities the citizens’ assembly that governed civic matters (Acts 19:39), and in the Septuagint the assembly (qahal) of Israel. It was a Greek civic institution rather than a Roman colonial instrument.

words.claimed: Sent ones whom Rome sent from the kingdom to set up an ekklēsia and convert a colony.
words.lexicon: Messenger, envoy, one sent; in classical Greek also a naval expedition. There is no evidence it was a Roman title for officials who founded colonial assemblies.

questions.q: Why does the series say approaching church as a provider of needs leads to disappointment?
questions.a: Because the church is not for meeting needs but for producing mature sons. It is meant to confront, challenge, change and hold you accountable, and families gather around covenant rather than need.

questions.q: How does this part define the glory of God?
questions.a: Not as clouds or felt presence but as God’s intention made manifest: Jesus become flesh, creation and humanity itself. So the earth full of glory means people knowing who they are.

questions.q: What was the Roman strategy the preacher sees behind ekklēsia and apostles?
questions.a: Instead of plundering conquered lands, Rome sent envoys to set up a governing assembly that replaced the local system and made the colony like the empire. Jesus used this picture: the church turns its region into heaven.

questions.q: What does it mean to discern the body?
questions.a: To see one another as God sees us, regarding no one according to the flesh and recognising what each carries. Failure to do this, with judgment and bitterness, is linked to weakness, sickness and death.

questions.q: What does the Nazareth story teach about familiarity?
questions.a: The people moved from astonished to offended when they recalled Jesus’ family, seeing Him as a mere man, and so He could do few miracles there. Familiarity plus immaturity breeds contempt and blocks impartation.

questions.q: Why should Christians not try to create unity?
questions.a: Because unity already exists in heaven’s Zion; attempts to manufacture it reduce everything to the lowest common denominator. Believers are told to preserve it by looking past doctrine and preference and gathering as family.

questions.q: What is the difference between power and authority here?
questions.a: Power comes from God, while authority is conferred within the body and holds the local church together. Jesus was empowered by the Father but authorised by His cousin John.

questions.q: Why is John the Revelator held up as a model?
questions.a: He saw both the risen Christ and the resurrected bride, discerned the body, and wrote that as He is so are we; the preacher links this to his not dying.

practice: Show up to your local church as family, not only when you need something.
Receive challenge and accountability from your church rather than expecting it to serve your needs.
Take responsibility for your town or region as your sphere, bringing heaven’s culture into it.
See the person next to you as the risen Christ sees them, not by their past, family or flaws.
Honour leaders and fellow believers so you can receive what they carry.
Love others as Christ loves you, not in proportion to how they treat you.
Preserve unity by looking past pet doctrines and preferences; don’t gather around agreement.
Attend the larger gathering for teaching and meet in homes with friends for fellowship.
Value in‑person impartation over livestreams and online courses alone.

fair.claim: John the Revelator has no death record, Jesus affirmed he would not die, and attempts to kill him failed, linked to his discerning the body.
fair.note: John 21:23 itself says Jesus did not say John would not die; the Gospel writer corrects exactly this rumour. Early tradition (Irenaeus, Polycrates of Ephesus) records John dying of old age in Ephesus around AD 100, with a tomb there; the boiling‑oil story is a later legend (Tertullian). Scripture teaches that all people die until Christ returns. Charitable reading: John’s long life and survival of persecution are well attested, and the preacher may be stressing life in Christ rather than literal deathlessness.
An early (pre‑70) date is held by preterist scholars, but most scholars follow Irenaeus in dating it around AD 95 under Domitian. It is a genuine debate, not settled.

fair.claim: John fell down as dead twice: before the risen Christ and before the resurrected bride.
fair.note: John falls as dead before Christ in Rev 1:17, but his other two falls (Rev 19:10; 22:8) are before an angel, whom he is told not to worship; no text shows him falling at the sight of the bride in Rev 21.

fair.claim: John calls himself “the Beloved” in his letter.
fair.note: The phrase “the disciple whom Jesus loved” is from the Gospel of John (John 13:23; 21:20). In the letters John addresses his readers as “beloved” but does not call himself that.

fair.claim: Moses saw God’s “back parts,” which in Hebrew means times past, i.e. creation itself; God’s glory is humanity.
fair.note: ʾāḥôr means “back” and, temporally, more often “afterward” than “past.” In Exod 33–34 God answers the request for glory by proclaiming His goodness and name (merciful, gracious, abounding in love). Scripture does call humans God’s image and glory (1 Cor 11:7; Ps 8:5), and Christ the radiance of His glory (Heb 1:3), but most theology distinguishes God’s own glory from the creatures who reflect it (Isa 42:8). Reading the rock as Christ has a long typological history.

This paraphrases Hab 1:13, but in the same verse Habakkuk asks why God does look on the treacherous; elsewhere God sees all things (Heb 4:13). The phrase is about God not tolerating evil rather than being unable to see it. The preacher uses it to say God is not repelled by people, a point many would affirm.

fair.claim: The gospel’s end goal is that all humans become the manifestation of the Godhead; one died for all, so all died and the world’s sin is already removed.
fair.note: The universal scope of Christ’s death is affirmed by many (2 Cor 5:14–15; 1 John 2:2), but most traditions hold that reconciliation must be received through faith (2 Cor 5:20 “be reconciled”; John 3:18, 36). “Fullness of God” (Eph 3:19) is prayed for believers, and the creature–Creator distinction remains. These are core debates between Christian universalism and mainstream positions.

fair.claim: The greatest commandment (love God and neighbour) is null now that Jesus fulfilled the Law; the new commandment is the only time Jesus tells us what to do.
fair.note: The New Testament repeatedly restates love of neighbour as fulfilling the law for believers (Rom 13:8–10; Gal 5:14; Jas 2:8), and Jesus commanded disciples to teach all He commanded (Matt 28:20). Also, the “Golden Rule” is Matt 7:12, not the greatest commandment, and John 13:34 says “love one another,” not “love your neighbour.” Charitable reading: the new commandment does raise the standard from “as yourself” to “as I have loved you.”

fair.claim: Paul says at the end of Romans that he must come to Rome to impart something and bear fruit.
fair.note: The wish to impart a spiritual gift and reap fruit is at the start of the letter (Rom 1:11–13); the end (Rom 15:23–32) mentions travel plans. The point that Paul valued personal presence stands.

fair.claim: Ekklēsia and apostolos were Roman military/colonial terms; Rome conquered by sending apostles to set up an ekklēsia in each colony, and the Lord’s Prayer reflects this.
fair.note: Ekklēsia was the Greek civic assembly of citizens (and the Septuagint word for Israel’s congregation); Roman colonies were governed by councils of decurions and magistrates, not ekklēsiai, and apostolos was not a Roman colonial office. The comparison of Egyptian and Roman warfare is a simplification. The Lord’s Prayer says “on earth as in heaven.” Charitable reading: Phil 3:20 (citizenship in heaven) and Philippi’s status as a Roman colony do support a colony analogy as an illustration.

fair.claim: Many are weak, sick and dying because they don’t discern the body, meaning they don’t see one another as God sees them.
fair.note: In 1 Cor 11 the warning is about the Lord’s Supper, and “sleep” means died. Interpreters differ: some read “body” as Christ’s body in the bread, others (with good contextual support, see 1 Cor 10:17; 11:21–22, 33) as the church community the Corinthians were dividing. The preacher’s corporate reading has respectable support, though he drops the Eucharistic setting.

fair.claim: Power comes from God, but authority does not; Jesus was authorised by His cousin John.
fair.note: Scripture says all authority comes from God (Rom 13:1) and that the Father gave Jesus all authority (Matt 28:18; John 5:27). However, some scholars do read Matt 21:23–27 as Jesus implicitly linking His mission to John’s prophetic baptism, so the preacher’s reading is not without support. John being exactly six months into ministry is a traditional inference, not stated in the text.

fair.claim: The church in Ephesus had 26,000 members and early believers sat under apostolic teaching in gatherings of 26,000 and up.
fair.note: There is no ancient evidence for the size of the Ephesian church; Acts records about 3,000 and later 5,000 men in Jerusalem (Acts 2:41; 4:4). The point that early churches combined larger gatherings (temple courts) with house meetings is supported by Acts 2:46.
This is a popular modern claim based on the temple‑tax story and rabbinic customs; the Gospels do not give ages, and Peter was married. It is speculative.
